supply_chain_attacks.attack_name: Internal Package Name Collision via Public Registry
supply_chain_attacks.description: An attacker discovers the names of internal/private packages used by a target organization (through leaked lock files, job postings, or GitHub repositories) and publishes identically-named packages on a public registry with higher version numbers. Build systems configured to check both public and private registries may prefer the malicious public package due to version resolution policies.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: Alex Birsan's 2021 research demonstrated dependency confusion against Apple, Microsoft, and PayPal by publishing packages with internal names to npm, PyPI, and RubyGems. Over 35 organizations were affected, with code execution achieved on internal build servers.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Remote code execution during package installation or build process. Attacker gains access to internal build infrastructure, can exfiltrate secrets, source code, and credentials.
detection_methods: Monitor public registries for packages matching internal package names
Alert on dependency resolution changes in lock files
Network monitoring for unexpected outbound connections during builds
Audit package sources in CI/CD logs
mitigations: Use scoped packages (@org/package-name) on npm
Configure package managers to use private registry exclusively for internal packages
Pin dependencies with integrity hashes in lock files
Implement pre-install scripts that verify package origin
Use tools like Socket.dev or Snyk to detect dependency confusion
supply_chain_attacks.keywords: dependency confusion,namespace collision,private packages,version resolution,internal names

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers exploit the difference between scoped (@scope/package) and unscoped npm packages. When an organization uses scoped packages internally but references them without the scope in some configurations, attackers register the unscoped variant on the public npm registry. Alternatively, attackers register scopes that are visually similar to legitimate organizational scopes.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: Multiple incidents where organizations using internal scoped packages had build systems that incorrectly resolved unscoped variants from the public npm registry, leading to installation of attacker-controlled packages.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Execution of malicious code during npm install. Can lead to credential theft, data exfiltration, or backdoor installation in built artifacts.
detection_methods: Verify all dependencies resolve from expected registries
Monitor for packages published under similar scope names
Audit .npmrc configuration across all projects
Use npm audit signatures to verify package provenance
mitigations: Always use scoped packages with organizationally-controlled scopes
Configure .npmrc to route scoped packages to private registry
Use npm config set registry to specify the default registry
Implement package-lock.json integrity checking with npm ci

supply_chain_attacks.description: In Java/Maven ecosystems, attackers publish artifacts with the same group ID and artifact ID as internal packages to Maven Central or other public repositories. Maven's repository ordering determines resolution priority, and misconfigured settings.xml or pom.xml files may cause Maven to prefer the public repository version over the internal Nexus/Artifactory version.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: Researchers demonstrated that many organizations using internal Maven repositories with custom group IDs were vulnerable when the same group IDs were not reserved on Maven Central, allowing attackers to publish malicious artifacts.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Malicious code execution during build. Particularly dangerous in Maven as build plugins can execute arbitrary code with full build system access.
detection_methods: Audit Maven settings.xml for repository ordering
Monitor Maven Central for artifacts matching internal group IDs
Verify artifact signatures and checksums during build
Use repository manager (Nexus/Artifactory) virtual repositories with proper routing
mitigations: Reserve internal group IDs on Maven Central
Configure repository manager to proxy only approved remote repositories
Use Gradle's repository content filtering
Implement dependency verification with checksums in Gradle
Use Maven Enforcer plugin to restrict allowed repositories

supply_chain_attacks.attack_name: PyPI Dependency Confusion via Extra Index URLs
supply_chain_attacks.description: Python's pip tool supports multiple package indices via --extra-index-url. When a private index is configured as an extra index (not the primary), pip may install the highest version from any index, including PyPI. Attackers publish packages with the same name as internal packages to PyPI with inflated version numbers, causing pip to prefer the malicious public package.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: The original Alex Birsan research specifically targeted Python's pip with extra-index-url, demonstrating that the highest version from any configured index would be installed. This affected organizations including Microsoft and Apple.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Arbitrary code execution during pip install via setup.py. Python's setup.py executes during installation, providing immediate code execution without requiring the package to be imported.
detection_methods: Audit pip.conf and requirements.txt for extra-index-url usage
Monitor PyPI for packages matching internal package names
Use pip install --require-hashes to enforce expected packages
Scan installed packages against expected package sources
mitigations: Use --index-url (not --extra-index-url) pointing to a private repository that proxies PyPI
Use pip install --require-hashes for all dependencies
Configure private PyPI (devpi, Artifactory) as the sole index with curated upstream packages
Register internal package names on PyPI as placeholders

supply_chain_attacks.description: In Go's module system, modules are identified by their repository path (e.g., github.com/org/module). While Go modules are tied to VCS paths making traditional dependency confusion harder, attackers can exploit misconfigured GOPROXY settings, vanity import paths, or organizations that use custom module paths without proper GONOSUMDB configuration to serve malicious modules.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: Research has shown that Go modules using vanity import paths (e.g., company.com/module) can be vulnerable if the vanity path server is compromised or if the module is not properly registered in the Go checksum database (sum.golang.org).
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Malicious code execution during go build. Go's init() functions execute automatically when a package is imported, providing a code execution vector.
detection_methods: Verify go.sum file integrity
Monitor GOPROXY access logs for unexpected module requests
Audit GONOSUMDB and GONOSUMCHECK configurations
Verify module sources match expected repositories
mitigations: Use GONOSUMDB only for truly private modules
Configure GOPROXY to use a private module proxy (Athens, Go Module Mirror)
Verify go.sum hashes in CI/CD pipelines
Use GOFLAGS=-mod=vendor for hermetic builds with vendored dependencies

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers register package names that differ from popular packages by substituting visually similar characters (e.g., replacing 'l' with '1', 'o' with '0', 'rn' with 'm'). Developers who mistype package names during installation unknowingly install the malicious package. The malicious package typically includes the legitimate package's functionality to avoid detection while executing additional malicious code.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: In 2017, the 'crossenv' package on npm (typosquat of 'cross-env') was discovered stealing environment variables including npm tokens. It had been downloaded over 700 times before detection.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Data exfiltration (environment variables, tokens, credentials), cryptocurrency mining, backdoor installation. Impact depends on the attacker's payload and the privileges of the installation context.
detection_methods: Use typosquatting detection tools (e.g., Socket.dev, OSSFuzz)
Implement package allowlisting in CI/CD pipelines
Review dependency additions in code review
Monitor for unusual packages in lock file diffs
mitigations: Copy-paste package names from official documentation instead of typing
Use lock files to pin exact dependency versions
Implement package approval workflows for new dependencies
Use IDE extensions that warn about suspicious package names

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers register package names with transposed characters (e.g., 'reqeusts' instead of 'requests', 'axois' instead of 'axios'). This targets common typing errors where adjacent characters are swapped. The technique is particularly effective for long package names where transposition errors are hard to spot visually.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: Multiple PyPI typosquatting campaigns have been discovered using transposed characters of popular packages like 'requesrs' and 'requsets' (targeting 'requests'), which collectively had thousands of downloads.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Code execution during installation. Payloads range from credential theft to reverse shells. Some typosquats include the legitimate package as a dependency to maintain functionality and avoid detection.
detection_methods: Levenshtein distance analysis against popular package names
Registry-level typosquatting detection (PyPI, npm have deployed this)
Pre-commit hooks that verify package names against an allowlist
Automated dependency review tools
mitigations: Use lock files with integrity verification
Implement dependency review as part of code review process
Use allowlists for permitted packages in enterprise environments
Enable npm audit signatures for provenance verification

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers exploit ambiguity in package naming conventions around separators (hyphens, underscores, periods). For example, registering 'python_dateutil' when the legitimate package is 'python-dateutil', or 'setup-tools' when the legitimate package is 'setuptools'. Package managers may normalize separators differently, creating opportunities for confusion.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: PyPI has seen numerous separator confusion attacks. PEP 503 specifies that PyPI normalizes package names (replacing hyphens, underscores, and periods with hyphens), but pip does not always enforce this during install, creating windows for confusion.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Installation of malicious package with attacker-controlled code execution. Particularly dangerous because the name difference is extremely subtle and often overlooked in code review.
detection_methods: Normalize package names before comparison in security tools
Use registry-provided package normalization APIs
Automated analysis of dependency additions for separator variants
Compare against canonical package names from official sources
mitigations: Always use the canonical package name from official documentation
Use lock files that record the resolved canonical name
Implement package name normalization in internal tools
Configure package managers to use strict name matching where available

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers register package names that omit a word from or add a word to a legitimate package name (e.g., 'python-nmap' vs 'nmap', 'react-dev-utils' vs 'react-dev-util'). This targets developers who may not remember the exact multi-word package name. The technique is especially effective for packages with common prefixes like 'python-', 'node-', or 'react-'.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: In 2022, researchers found over 200 malicious npm packages using word omission/addition typosquatting targeting popular packages. Packages like 'react-dev-util' (missing final 's') contained cryptocurrency-stealing malware.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Malicious code execution during installation or import. Attackers may include the legitimate package as a dependency to maintain expected functionality while running malicious code in parallel.
detection_methods: Fuzzy matching of new dependencies against known-good package databases
CI/CD checks that compare added dependencies against approved lists
Manual review of dependency additions in pull requests
Monitoring package download anomalies
mitigations: Use exact package names from official documentation or registry
Implement dependency approval workflows
Pin dependencies in lock files with integrity verification
Use organization-wide approved dependency lists

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers publish packages using the name or branding of well-known organizations or projects to appear legitimate (e.g., 'azure-core-security', 'google-auth-helper', 'aws-lambda-utils'). These packages impersonate official packages from major technology companies and may include convincing README files, documentation, and even functional code to maintain the deception.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: In 2023, researchers discovered hundreds of malicious packages on npm and PyPI impersonating Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and AWS packages. These packages used convincing descriptions and README content generated by AI to appear legitimate.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Credential theft targeting cloud provider credentials (AWS access keys, Azure tokens, GCP service account keys). Data exfiltration of environment variables and configuration files.
detection_methods: Verify package publisher identity matches the claimed organization
Check package age, download counts, and community indicators
Verify packages against official SDK documentation
Use registry verified publisher badges where available
mitigations: Only install packages listed in official documentation from the vendor
Verify publisher identity on the registry (npm verified publishers, PyPI Trusted Publishers)
Use organization-curated internal registries
Implement automated checks for brand impersonation in CI/CD

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers compromise the account credentials of a legitimate package maintainer through credential stuffing, phishing, or exploiting password reuse. Once the maintainer account is controlled, the attacker publishes malicious versions of the maintainer's packages. This is particularly dangerous because the packages are genuinely published by the legitimate maintainer account, making detection extremely difficult.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: The ua-parser-js incident (October 2021) involved the takeover of the npm maintainer account, leading to the publication of malicious versions (0.7.29, 0.8.0, 1.0.0) containing cryptocurrency mining and credential-stealing malware. The package had 8 million weekly downloads.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Massive downstream impact due to the package's existing trust and user base. Malicious code executes in all environments that update to the compromised version, including CI/CD pipelines, production servers, and developer workstations.
detection_methods: Monitor for unexpected version publications of critical dependencies
Analyze behavioral changes between package versions (new network calls, file access)
Enable npm audit signatures to detect unsigned publications
Monitor package publication patterns for anomalous timing or content
mitigations: Require MFA for all package registry accounts
Use npm provenance and PyPI attestations to verify build origin
Pin dependency versions and review updates before adoption
Implement automated behavioral analysis of package updates
Enable registry notifications for package updates

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers build trust with open source maintainers over time by contributing legitimate code, helping with issue triage, and engaging positively in the community. After establishing trust, the attacker requests and receives maintainer access. Once granted elevated permissions, the attacker introduces malicious code either directly or through subtle, hard-to-detect backdoors hidden within seemingly legitimate contributions.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: The xz-utils backdoor (CVE-2024-3094, March 2024) was the most sophisticated known supply chain attack. The attacker 'Jia Tan' spent over two years building trust with the xz-utils maintainer, gradually gaining commit access, and ultimately inserting an obfuscated backdoor targeting OpenSSH authentication on Linux systems. The backdoor was discovered by chance through performance anomalies.
supply_chain_attacks.affected_ecosystem: All open source ecosystems, particularly single-maintainer projects
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Complete system compromise. The xz-utils backdoor would have provided unauthorized remote access to millions of Linux systems. Social engineering attacks can persist undetected for years due to the trust relationship.
detection_methods: Behavioral analysis of contributor patterns over time
Code review for obfuscated or unnecessarily complex code
Monitor for changes to build scripts and test infrastructure
Verify that binary test fixtures match their purported content
mitigations: Require multiple independent reviewers for sensitive code areas
Implement CODEOWNERS for security-critical files
Use reproducible builds to verify build output matches source
Monitor for changes to build infrastructure and test fixtures
Maintain a bus factor greater than 1 for critical projects

supply_chain_attacks.attack_name: Maintainer Token Theft via CI/CD Exposure
supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers steal package registry authentication tokens (npm tokens, PyPI API keys) that are accidentally exposed in CI/CD configurations, environment variables, log files, or source code. Exposed tokens allow attackers to publish new versions of the maintainer's packages without needing to compromise the maintainer's account directly. CI/CD environments are particularly high-value targets as they often contain publishing credentials.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: In 2021, researchers found thousands of npm tokens exposed in public GitHub repositories, CI/CD configurations, and log files. Some of these tokens had publish access to popular packages with millions of weekly downloads.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Attacker can publish malicious versions of any package the token has access to. Impact scales with the popularity and trust level of the affected packages.
detection_methods: Secret scanning in source code and CI/CD configurations (Gitleaks, truffleHog)
Monitor package publications for unexpected source IPs or user agents
Registry audit logs showing token usage from unusual locations
Automated detection of tokens in build logs
mitigations: Use short-lived, scoped tokens for CI/CD publishing
Implement secret scanning in all repositories and CI/CD pipelines
Use OIDC-based publishing (npm provenance, PyPI Trusted Publishers)
Rotate tokens regularly and revoke exposed tokens immediately
Configure CI/CD to mask secrets in log output

supply_chain_attacks.description: A trusted maintainer intentionally introduces malicious code into a package they legitimately maintain. Unlike social engineering attacks, the maintainer has always had access and may be motivated by financial gain, ideology, or coercion. The malicious code may be introduced gradually through small, innocuous-looking changes that collectively form a backdoor or through obfuscated code hidden in complex logic.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: The 'colors.js' and 'faker.js' incident (January 2022) involved the maintainer Marak Squires deliberately sabotaging his own packages in protest, adding infinite loops that printed garbage text. While this was protest-ware rather than malicious exploitation, it demonstrated the single-point-of-failure risk of maintainer trust.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Ranges from service disruption (protest-ware) to complete system compromise (backdoor). Insider threats are extremely difficult to detect because the code passes all authentication and authorization checks.
detection_methods: Behavioral analysis of code changes (entropy analysis, new capabilities)
Automated detection of obfuscated code or unusual patterns
Independent code review by multiple maintainers
Runtime behavioral monitoring of package execution
mitigations: Require multi-maintainer review for all changes
Use reproducible builds to enable independent verification
Implement behavioral monitoring in production environments
Diversify critical dependencies to reduce single-maintainer risk
Support open source maintainers to reduce burnout-driven risks

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers acquire expired or available email domains previously used by package maintainers. They then use the acquired domain to reset passwords on package registry accounts, gaining full control of the maintainer's registry identity. This technique targets the weakest link in account recovery processes and can affect maintainers who used custom domains that have since expired.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: Research by academic teams has shown that a significant percentage of npm package maintainers use email addresses on domains that have expired and are available for purchase, potentially affecting packages with millions of weekly downloads.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Full account takeover enabling publication of malicious package versions. The attacker assumes the legitimate maintainer's identity, making detection extremely difficult.
detection_methods: Monitor maintainer email domain expiration dates
Registry-side detection of password resets from newly registered domains
Alert on publications from maintainer accounts after long periods of inactivity
Domain registrar monitoring for domains associated with critical packages
mitigations: Require MFA on all registry accounts (prevents email-only recovery)
Registries should implement additional verification for dormant account recovery
Maintainers should use email addresses on stable, long-term domains
Organizations should monitor email domain status of critical dependency maintainers
supply_chain_attacks.keywords: email domain,domain takeover,account recovery,password reset,expired domain

supply_chain_attacks.description: The event-stream npm package was compromised when a new maintainer (right9ctrl) who had gained trust through contributions added a dependency on 'flatmap-stream', which contained encrypted malicious code targeting the Copay Bitcoin wallet. The malware specifically activated only in the Copay application context, decrypting and executing code that would steal cryptocurrency wallet credentials.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: event-stream (npm) was compromised in September 2018. The attacker social-engineered maintainer access, then added the 'flatmap-stream' dependency which contained AES-encrypted malicious code. The code was designed to activate only within the Copay Bitcoin wallet app, making detection extremely difficult. Discovered by a community member reviewing the dependency.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Targeted cryptocurrency theft from Copay wallet users. Broader impact: demonstrated the viability of targeted supply chain attacks through popular packages with large dependency trees.
detection_methods: Review new dependencies added to packages
Analyze encrypted or obfuscated code in dependencies
Behavioral analysis of package code for environment-specific activation
Monitor for unexpected AES decryption or eval() calls in dependencies
mitigations: Review and audit all new dependencies before adoption
Monitor dependency changes in popular packages
Use SCA tools that analyze dependency behavior, not just known vulnerabilities
Implement runtime application self-protection (RASP) for sensitive operations

supply_chain_attacks.description: The ua-parser-js npm package (8 million weekly downloads) was compromised through maintainer account takeover. Malicious versions were published containing a cryptocurrency miner and a credential-stealing trojan for both Linux and Windows platforms. The malware was embedded in the package's postinstall script, ensuring automatic execution upon installation.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: In October 2021, three malicious versions of ua-parser-js (0.7.29, 0.8.0, 1.0.0) were published containing a cryptominer (jsextension) for Linux and a credential stealer (create.dll) for Windows. The compromise was discovered within hours, but the affected versions were downloaded thousands of times.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Cryptocurrency mining consuming compute resources. Credential theft on Windows systems. Any system that ran npm install with the affected versions was compromised. CI/CD systems and production servers were affected.
detection_methods: Monitor for unexpected binary downloads during npm install
Analyze postinstall scripts for suspicious behavior
Detect crypto-mining processes on build servers
Alert on unexpected network connections during package installation
mitigations: Pin exact dependency versions in package-lock.json
Use npm ci instead of npm install in CI/CD
Implement runtime monitoring on build servers
Use --ignore-scripts flag where possible
Review package updates before adoption using npm diff

supply_chain_attacks.description: The maintainer of the widely-used colors.js and faker.js npm packages deliberately sabotaged them in January 2022 as a protest against large corporations using open source without adequate compensation. Colors.js was modified to print an infinite loop of garbled text (LIBERTY LIBERTY LIBERTY), while faker.js was emptied entirely. This affected thousands of applications including the AWS CDK.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: In January 2022, Marak Squires published colors.js v1.4.1 with an infinite loop and faker.js v6.6.6 with all code removed. Colors.js had 23 million weekly downloads. The sabotage caused widespread CI/CD failures and highlighted the sustainability crisis in open source software.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Denial of service: applications using colors.js entered infinite loops. Applications using faker.js lost all functionality. CI/CD pipelines failed across thousands of organizations. Highlighted the fragility of the open source supply chain.
detection_methods: Monitor for sudden major version bumps or unexpected releases
Analyze code changes in dependency updates
CI/CD timeout detection for infinite loop scenarios
Community monitoring and alerting for popular package changes
mitigations: Pin dependency versions in lock files
Do not auto-update dependencies without review
Implement CI/CD timeouts for build and test phases
Maintain forks of critical dependencies as fallback
Support open source maintainers financially to reduce sustainability risks

supply_chain_attacks.description: The maintainer of node-ipc (npm package with 1 million weekly downloads) added the 'peacenotwar' module that, when executed on systems with Russian or Belarusian IP addresses, would overwrite files with heart emojis as an anti-war protest. This geo-targeted destructive behavior represented a dangerous escalation of protestware into data destruction.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: In March 2022, node-ipc versions 10.1.1 and 10.1.2 contained code that checked the user's IP geolocation and, for Russian/Belarusian IPs, overwrote arbitrary files with heart emojis. The package was a dependency of vue-cli, affecting a massive number of Vue.js developers. CVE-2022-23812 was assigned.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Data destruction for users in targeted geographies. Erosion of trust in the open source supply chain. Demonstrated that maintainers with political motivations can weaponize their packages for geo-targeted attacks.
detection_methods: Behavioral analysis detecting geolocation checks in packages
File integrity monitoring on development systems
Network monitoring for geolocation API calls during builds
Automated analysis of package updates for destructive operations
mitigations: Pin dependency versions and review all updates
Run builds in isolated environments with network restrictions
Implement file integrity monitoring on build systems
Use SCA tools that detect behavioral anomalies, not just CVEs
Sandbox package installation using tools like Sandworm

supply_chain_attacks.attack_name: Malicious PyPI Packages with Data Exfiltration
supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers publish packages to PyPI that contain data exfiltration capabilities in their setup.py or __init__.py files. Upon installation, these packages collect sensitive information including environment variables, SSH keys, AWS credentials, browser cookies, and system information, and transmit them to attacker-controlled servers. Campaigns often publish dozens of packages simultaneously.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: Phylum and Checkmarx have documented numerous campaigns where hundreds of malicious PyPI packages were published in bursts, targeting developers with data-stealing code. Notable campaigns include 'W4SP Stealer' (2022-2023) which exfiltrated Discord tokens, browser passwords, and cryptocurrency wallets.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Theft of credentials, API keys, SSH keys, cryptocurrency wallets, and browser data. Compromised development environments can lead to further supply chain attacks if stolen credentials provide access to package registries or code repositories.
detection_methods: Monitor setup.py for network calls and file system access
Analyze packages for base64-encoded or obfuscated payloads
Detect webhook URLs (Discord, Telegram) in package code
Use PyPI malware detection services (e.g., PyPI's own malware checks)
mitigations: Use pip install --require-hashes for all dependencies
Install packages in isolated virtual environments
Run security scanners on all new dependencies before adoption
Use container-based development environments with restricted network access
Monitor outbound network connections from development environments

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers publish npm packages or compromise existing ones to include cryptocurrency mining code that activates on the victim's machine. The mining code may be in the package itself or downloaded at runtime from an external server. Some variants only activate during CI/CD builds to exploit the compute resources of cloud-based build infrastructure without being noticed on developer workstations.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: In 2018, the 'event-stream' compromise included a cryptominer targeting Copay wallets. In 2019, the 'bb-builder' and 'discord.js-user' packages contained XMRig cryptocurrency miners. Multiple subsequent campaigns have targeted npm with cryptomining payloads.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Unauthorized consumption of compute resources, increased cloud costs, degraded build performance. In CI/CD environments, crypto mining may slow builds significantly and increase cloud bills. May also indicate other malicious activity.
detection_methods: Monitor CPU usage during package installation and build
Detect known mining pool connections in network traffic
Scan for cryptocurrency mining binaries (XMRig, CGMiner) in packages
Alert on unusual compute resource consumption in CI/CD
mitigations: Use --ignore-scripts where feasible to prevent postinstall execution
Monitor resource consumption in CI/CD environments
Implement network egress controls blocking known mining pools
Use containerized builds with CPU/memory limits
Scan packages for binary payloads before installation

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers leverage npm's lifecycle scripts (preinstall, install, postinstall) to execute arbitrary code during package installation. These scripts run automatically unless explicitly disabled, providing an immediate code execution vector. Malicious postinstall scripts can download and execute payloads, modify system files, establish persistence, or exfiltrate data -- all triggered by a simple 'npm install'.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: A large number of malicious npm packages use postinstall scripts as their primary execution vector. Notable examples include 'eslint-scope' (compromised legitimate package, 2018), where the postinstall script downloaded a credential-stealing payload.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Immediate arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the user running npm install. In CI/CD environments, this often means root or admin privileges with access to deployment credentials and secrets.
detection_methods: Audit package.json for lifecycle scripts before installation
Use npm explain to understand why a package is being installed
Monitor process execution during npm install for unexpected child processes
Use Socket.dev or similar tools that analyze install scripts
mitigations: Use --ignore-scripts flag for npm install where possible
Audit all packages that include install scripts
Use npm ci in CI/CD (respects lock file exactly)
Configure npm to ignore scripts globally and whitelist known-good packages
Use Corepack to manage package managers securely

supply_chain_attacks.description: State-sponsored attackers (attributed to Russian SVR) compromised SolarWinds' build infrastructure and injected a sophisticated backdoor (SUNBURST) into the Orion IT monitoring platform. The malicious code was inserted during the build process and distributed through legitimate software updates signed by SolarWinds' code signing certificate, making it appear completely authentic to customers.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: Discovered in December 2020, the SUNBURST backdoor had been distributed in SolarWinds Orion versions 2019.4 HF 5 through 2020.2.1 (March-June 2020). An estimated 18,000 customers installed the trojanized update. The attack compromised multiple US government agencies and major corporations. It remained undetected for approximately 9 months.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Nation-state espionage affecting 18,000+ organizations including US Treasury, Commerce, and Homeland Security departments. Demonstrated that build system compromise can bypass all downstream security controls including code signing and update verification.
detection_methods: Anomalous DNS queries to avsvmcloud.com C2 domain
Behavioral analysis of Orion process network activity
Memory forensics for SUNBURST indicators
Build system integrity monitoring (would have detected unauthorized build modifications)
mitigations: Implement SLSA Level 3+ build integrity controls
Use reproducible builds to detect build-time tampering
Monitor build systems for unauthorized modifications
Implement zero-trust architecture for internal networks
Deploy EDR with behavioral detection capabilities

supply_chain_attacks.attack_name: Codecov Supply Chain Attack (Bash Uploader Compromise)
supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers modified the Codecov Bash Uploader script that customers download and execute in their CI/CD pipelines. The modified script exfiltrated environment variables (including CI/CD secrets, API tokens, and credentials) from the build environment to an attacker-controlled server. The attack was enabled by unauthorized access to Codecov's Docker image creation process.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: In January 2021, attackers exploited a flaw in Codecov's Docker image creation process to modify the Bash Uploader script hosted at codecov.io/bash. The modified script added a single line that exfiltrated all environment variables to the attacker's server. The compromise was not discovered until April 2021, affecting thousands of CI/CD pipelines.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Theft of all environment variables from CI/CD pipelines, including API tokens, cloud credentials, package registry tokens, and other secrets. Affected organizations included Twitch, HashiCorp, Confluent, and many others. Led to credential rotation across thousands of organizations.
detection_methods: Verify integrity of downloaded scripts using checksums before execution
Monitor CI/CD environment variables for exfiltration attempts
Network monitoring for unexpected outbound connections during builds
Audit changes to CI/CD pipeline configurations
mitigations: Verify checksums of all scripts downloaded and executed in CI/CD
Pin specific versions of CI/CD tools and verify their integrity
Use OIDC tokens instead of long-lived secrets in CI/CD
Implement network egress controls on build environments
Minimize secrets available to CI/CD environments

supply_chain_attacks.description: A sophisticated supply chain attack targeting the xz compression library used by OpenSSH on Linux systems. The attacker 'Jia Tan' spent over two years building trust as a contributor, eventually becoming a co-maintainer. Malicious code was hidden in binary test fixtures and activated through the build system, ultimately modifying the behavior of OpenSSH's sshd to allow unauthorized authentication, effectively creating an RCE backdoor accessible to anyone with the attacker's private key.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: Discovered in March 2024 by Andres Freund (Microsoft) who noticed a 500ms latency increase in SSH connections. The backdoor in xz-utils 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 targeted the RSA authentication path in OpenSSH via the systemd linkage to liblzma. Only bleeding-edge Linux distributions (Fedora 41, Debian Sid) shipped the affected versions before discovery. Affected versions: 5.6.0, 5.6.1.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Potential for unauthorized remote access to any Linux system running the backdoored version. If the attack had reached stable distributions, it would have compromised millions of SSH servers worldwide. This is considered the most sophisticated public supply chain attack ever discovered.
detection_methods: Performance monitoring (the initial detection was via SSH latency regression)
Reproducible build verification (build output differed from source)
Binary analysis of test fixtures for hidden payloads
Behavioral analysis of ifunc resolvers and build system modifications
mitigations: Implement reproducible builds for critical infrastructure libraries
Require multiple independent reviewers for all changes
Verify that binary test fixtures match their purported content
Monitor build system modifications with the same rigor as source changes
Support maintainer sustainability to reduce burnout-driven trust delegation

supply_chain_attacks.attack_name: CI/CD Pipeline Poisoning via Pull Request
supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers submit pull requests to open source repositories that modify CI/CD workflow files to execute malicious code during the CI pipeline. If the repository's CI/CD is configured to run workflows on pull requests from forks without proper isolation (pwn_request vulnerability), the attacker's code runs with the repository's CI secrets and permissions.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: Researchers have demonstrated CI/CD pipeline poisoning against major open source projects including those maintained by Google, Microsoft, and Apache. GitHub's pull_request_target event and equivalent mechanisms in other CI platforms were commonly exploited before awareness improved.
supply_chain_attacks.affected_ecosystem: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure DevOps
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Access to CI/CD secrets (deployment credentials, signing keys, registry tokens). Ability to tamper with build output. Potential to publish malicious artifacts using stolen credentials.
detection_methods: Audit CI/CD workflow configurations for pull_request_target misuse
Monitor for workflow file modifications in pull requests
Review CI/CD permissions and secret exposure in workflow runs
Implement workflow-level secret scoping
mitigations: Use pull_request event (not pull_request_target) for fork PRs
Never checkout untrusted PR code in a context with secrets access
Use separate workflows for trusted (push) and untrusted (PR) events
Implement workflow approval requirements for first-time contributors
Scope CI/CD secrets to specific environments and workflows

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers compromise a build tool, compiler plugin, or build system dependency that is used during the software build process but not shipped in the final artifact. Because build tools have full access to the build environment, compromising them can inject malicious code into any software built with the tool. This creates a leverage point where a single compromised build tool affects all software built with it.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: The Codecov Bash Uploader compromise (2021) affected a build tool rather than a runtime dependency. The SolarWinds attack similarly compromised the build infrastructure. The hypothetical compromise of popular build tools like webpack, esbuild, or Gradle plugins would have massive downstream impact.
supply_chain_attacks.affected_ecosystem: All build ecosystems (npm/webpack, Maven/Gradle, pip/setuptools, cargo, go)
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Any software built with the compromised tool could contain injected malicious code. The malicious code appears in the final artifact even though the build tool is not listed as a runtime dependency, making it invisible to SCA tools that only examine the dependency tree.
detection_methods: Verify build tool integrity using checksums and signatures
Compare build output from multiple independent build environments
Monitor for unexpected build output changes between versions
Use reproducible builds to detect build-time code injection
mitigations: Pin build tool versions with integrity verification
Use hermetic builds that pre-fetch and verify all build inputs
Implement reproducible builds to enable output verification
Regularly audit build tool dependencies for vulnerabilities
Use SLSA Level 3+ build integrity controls

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers exploit the GitHub Actions cache mechanism to inject malicious content into cached build artifacts, dependencies, or tools. When a subsequent build restores the poisoned cache, the malicious content is used instead of the legitimate version. This can affect any build that shares the cache key, potentially across branches and even across forks in some configurations.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: Researchers demonstrated that GitHub Actions cache can be poisoned through various vectors: manipulating cache keys, exploiting the cache scope hierarchy, and injecting into shared caches. The attack persists across builds until the cache expires.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Build output contamination persisting across multiple builds. Compromised builds produce malicious artifacts that pass CI/CD checks because the cached malicious content is treated as trusted.
detection_methods: Verify cached artifact integrity after restoration
Monitor cache hit rates and content changes
Compare builds with and without cache to detect discrepancies
Audit cache key generation for predictability or manipulation
mitigations: Use content-addressable caching where possible
Verify integrity of restored cache entries
Limit cache sharing scope (branch-level isolation)
Regularly clear and rebuild caches
Use immutable caches that cannot be overwritten

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers target self-hosted CI/CD runners which, unlike hosted runners, persist between builds and may accumulate sensitive data, credentials, and build artifacts. Compromising a self-hosted runner provides persistent access to the build infrastructure, allowing the attacker to intercept secrets, modify builds, and inject malicious code into any software built on the runner.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: Multiple organizations have experienced self-hosted runner compromises where the persistent nature of the runner allowed attackers to collect secrets over time. GitHub's security documentation explicitly warns against using self-hosted runners for public repositories due to the risk of malicious fork PRs executing code on the runner.
supply_chain_attacks.affected_ecosystem: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, Azure DevOps
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Persistent access to build infrastructure. Ability to intercept all secrets used in builds, modify build output, and inject backdoors. Compromise persists until the runner is rebuilt from a clean state.
detection_methods: Monitor self-hosted runner health and integrity
Implement file integrity monitoring on runner systems
Detect unauthorized processes or network connections on runners
Audit runner registration and deregistration events
mitigations: Use ephemeral runners that are rebuilt for each job
Never use self-hosted runners for public repository workflows
Implement runner registration restrictions (organization/repository level)
Monitor runner systems with EDR solutions
Regularly rotate runner credentials and rebuild runner images

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers manipulate environment variables in the build environment to alter build behavior, inject malicious code, or redirect dependency resolution. Environment variables control critical build behaviors including compiler flags, dependency resolution paths, proxy settings, and authentication tokens. Injecting or modifying these variables can subtly alter the build output without modifying any source code.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: Build environment manipulation has been demonstrated through CI/CD variable injection, modifying PATH to intercept build tools, altering NODE_OPTIONS to inject code, and manipulating pip's PIP_INDEX_URL to redirect dependency downloads to attacker-controlled servers.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Build output manipulation, dependency redirection, credential interception. The attack is subtle because the source code remains unchanged, making code review ineffective for detection.
detection_methods: Audit environment variables at build start and compare to expected values
Monitor for unauthorized modifications to CI/CD variables
Log all environment variable values used during builds
Detect PATH modifications that introduce unexpected tool locations
mitigations: Define and validate expected environment variables at build start
Use hermetic builds that ignore external environment variables
Implement environment variable allowlisting in CI/CD
Use SLSA provenance to record environment variables used during builds
Restrict who can modify CI/CD environment variables

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers with write access to a repository modify the commit history to inject malicious code into past commits, making it appear as though the malicious code has always been present. Techniques include force-pushing rewritten history, amending past commits, and using interactive rebase to alter commit contents. Without commit signing verification, the modified history is indistinguishable from the original.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: While no major public incident has been attributed solely to history tampering, the technique is well-documented in security research. The PHP.net compromise (2021) involved direct commits to the php-src repository on git.php.net, demonstrating the risk of direct repository access without signing enforcement.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Malicious code appears to have been committed by legitimate developers in the past, making detection extremely difficult. Undermines the integrity of the entire commit history as a source of truth.
detection_methods: Enforce and verify GPG/SSH commit signatures
Monitor for force pushes on protected branches
Maintain external commit hash logs for comparison
Use Git server hooks to detect history rewrites
mitigations: Require signed commits on all protected branches
Disable force-push on protected branches
Use branch protection rules that prevent history modification
Maintain out-of-band records of commit hashes for critical repositories
Enable Git's receive.denyNonFastForwards and receive.denyDeletes

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers compromise the private keys used for GPG or SSH commit signing, enabling them to create commits that appear to be legitimately signed by a trusted developer. This defeats commit signature verification as a security control and allows the attacker to inject malicious code with a valid, trusted signature. Key compromise may occur through phishing, malware, or inadequate key storage security.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: While no major public supply chain attack has been specifically attributed to signing key compromise, the risk is well-documented. Sigstore and gitsign were created specifically to address the key management challenges of traditional GPG signing by using short-lived, OIDC-bound certificates instead of long-lived keys.
supply_chain_attacks.affected_ecosystem: All VCS systems using commit signing
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Attacker can create trusted commits that pass signature verification. All downstream security controls that rely on commit signing (branch protection, provenance) are bypassed. The attack is nearly undetectable without additional out-of-band verification.
detection_methods: Monitor for commits signed with compromised keys (requires revocation awareness)
Cross-reference signing timestamps with key issuance and revocation dates
Detect anomalous commit patterns (unusual times, large changes, out-of-character code)
Use transparency logs (Rekor) to audit signing events
mitigations: Use Sigstore gitsign for keyless, OIDC-based commit signing
Store signing keys in hardware security modules (YubiKey, TPM)
Implement key rotation and revocation procedures
Monitor signing events through transparency logs
Use short-lived signing certificates instead of long-lived GPG keys

supply_chain_attacks.attack_name: Unauthorized Direct Commit to Protected Branch
supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers bypass branch protection rules to commit directly to the main or production branch without going through the required review process. This can occur through misconfigured branch protection (admin bypass enabled), compromised admin accounts, or exploitation of VCS platform vulnerabilities. Direct commits bypass code review, CI/CD checks, and all other pull request-based security controls.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: The PHP.net compromise (March 2021) involved attackers pushing malicious commits directly to the php-src Git repository on git.php.net, impersonating legitimate PHP developers. The commits added a backdoor disguised as a typo fix. This led the PHP project to migrate from self-hosted Git to GitHub with stricter access controls.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Malicious code is merged directly into the production branch without review. The code will be included in the next release build and distributed to all users. Detection depends on post-merge code audit.
detection_methods: Alert on direct pushes to protected branches
Monitor Git server logs for push events bypassing PRs
Implement Git hooks that reject unsigned or unauthorized commits
Compare branch commit history against PR merge records
mitigations: Enable strict branch protection rules on all protected branches
Disable admin bypass of branch protection
Require pull request reviews from CODEOWNERS for all merges
Implement server-side pre-receive hooks that enforce signing and review
Use deploy keys with read-only access where possible

supply_chain_attacks.attack_name: Unicode and Homoglyph Code Injection (Trojan Source)
supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers use Unicode bidirectional control characters (Bidi overrides) to make source code appear different in text editors than how compilers interpret it. This allows malicious code to be hidden in plain sight during code review, as the reviewer sees benign logic while the compiler processes malicious logic. The technique can also use homoglyphs (visually identical characters from different Unicode blocks) to disguise variable names.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: The 'Trojan Source' attack was published by researchers from the University of Cambridge in November 2021 (CVE-2021-42574, CVE-2021-42694). They demonstrated that Unicode Bidi characters could reorder code logic in C, C++, JavaScript, Python, Go, Rust, and Java in ways invisible to human reviewers but meaningful to compilers.
supply_chain_attacks.affected_ecosystem: All programming languages that support Unicode
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Malicious code passes code review undetected because the malicious logic is visually hidden. The compiled/interpreted code behaves differently from what reviewers see, potentially introducing authentication bypasses, data leaks, or logic bombs.
detection_methods: Use source code editors and code review tools that highlight Unicode control characters
Implement pre-commit hooks that reject files containing Bidi control characters
Use linters that detect homoglyphs and invisible characters
Run compiller warnings for Unicode anomalies (-Wall -Wextra in GCC/Clang)
mitigations: Configure editors to display invisible/control characters
Implement pre-commit hooks rejecting Bidi control characters
Use linting rules that flag Unicode anomalies
Enable compiler warnings for Unicode-related issues
Review code in environments that render all Unicode control characters visibly

supply_chain_attacks.attack_name: Source Repository Compromise via GitHub App Exploitation
supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers exploit overly permissive GitHub Apps or OAuth apps installed on repositories to gain write access to source code, CI/CD workflows, or secrets. GitHub Apps with 'contents: write' permission can push commits, while apps with 'actions: write' can modify workflows. Compromising an app token provides silent, programmatic access that bypasses branch protection rules designed for human users.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: Multiple incidents have involved compromised GitHub App tokens being used to modify repository contents. The tj-actions/changed-files compromise (March 2025) demonstrated how a compromised GitHub Action could exfiltrate secrets from repositories that used it, affecting thousands of repositories.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Source code modification, secret exfiltration, workflow tampering. GitHub App tokens may bypass branch protection rules, allowing direct modifications to protected branches. Impact scales with the number of repositories the app is installed on.
detection_methods: Audit GitHub App permissions regularly
Monitor GitHub audit log for app-generated push events
Alert on modifications to CI/CD files from non-human actors
Review installed GitHub Apps for least-privilege compliance
mitigations: Apply least-privilege permissions to all GitHub Apps
Regularly audit installed apps and revoke unnecessary ones
Use fine-grained personal access tokens instead of classic tokens
Monitor audit logs for app-generated activities
Implement branch protection rules that also apply to app tokens

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers compromise the package registry infrastructure itself (npm, PyPI, Maven Central, etc.) to serve modified packages to all consumers. Unlike individual package compromise, registry-level compromise can affect any package on the platform and bypass all per-package verification mechanisms. This is the highest-impact supply chain attack vector but also the most difficult to execute.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: While no major public registry has been fully compromised, the risk is well-understood. The npm registry experienced a security incident in 2022 involving unauthorized access to internal systems. PHP's PEAR registry was compromised in 2019, with the main installation file (go-pear.phar) replaced with a backdoored version for 6 months.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Potentially affects every package on the registry and every user who downloads packages. The most catastrophic supply chain attack scenario. Can bypass all client-side verification if the registry's signing infrastructure is also compromised.
detection_methods: Verify package checksums against independent sources
Use package transparency logs (npm audit signatures, PyPI attestations)
Monitor for unexpected changes to package metadata or content
Cross-validate packages from multiple registry mirrors
mitigations: Use registry-provided integrity verification (npm audit signatures)
Pin dependencies with integrity hashes in lock files
Mirror critical packages in organization-controlled registries
Implement The Update Framework (TUF) for registry integrity
Use Sigstore to verify package provenance independently of the registry

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers compromise CDN nodes, package mirrors, or download servers that distribute software packages. By serving modified packages through legitimate distribution infrastructure, the attack can affect users who download from specific geographic regions or CDN edge nodes. The attack is difficult to detect because the download URL remains correct and the distribution infrastructure appears legitimate.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: In 2016, the Linux Mint website was compromised and the download link was replaced with a modified ISO containing a backdoor. Similar attacks have targeted PyPI mirrors, Homebrew bottles, and Linux distribution mirror networks. The attack surface is large because many mirrors operate independently with varying security postures.
supply_chain_attacks.affected_ecosystem: All software distribution systems using mirrors or CDNs
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Users downloading from compromised mirrors receive tampered software. The attack can be regionally targeted (specific CDN nodes) or time-limited, making forensic analysis difficult.
detection_methods: Verify download checksums against authoritative sources
Implement GPG signature verification for all downloads
Monitor CDN access logs for unusual patterns
Use certificate transparency to detect MitM on HTTPS downloads
mitigations: Always verify cryptographic signatures of downloaded software
Use TLS for all package downloads (reject HTTP fallback)
Implement The Update Framework (TUF) for tamper-evident distribution
Use content-addressable storage for immutable package distribution
Maintain hash databases independent of distribution infrastructure

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers intercept package downloads over insecure channels (HTTP, misconfigured TLS) and replace the legitimate package with a modified version containing malicious code. While most modern package managers use HTTPS by default, legacy configurations, corporate proxies, or TLS downgrade attacks can create opportunities for interception. This attack is particularly relevant in environments with corporate TLS inspection proxies.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: Research has shown that many package managers historically used HTTP for downloads, and some configurations still allow HTTP fallback. Corporate environments with TLS-intercepting proxies create additional attack surface if the proxy's CA certificate is compromised.
supply_chain_attacks.affected_ecosystem: All package ecosystems where HTTP or misconfigured TLS is possible
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Replacement of legitimate packages with malicious versions during download. The attack is transparent to the user unless integrity verification is performed after download.
detection_methods: Verify package integrity hashes after download
Monitor for HTTP (non-HTTPS) package registry connections
Detect TLS certificate anomalies for package registry connections
Compare downloaded package hashes against independent hash databases
mitigations: Enforce HTTPS for all package downloads (reject HTTP)
Use lock files with integrity hashes (npm ci, pip --require-hashes)
Implement certificate pinning for package registry connections where possible
Verify package signatures independently of the transport layer
Use private package mirrors within trusted networks

supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers exploit the mutable nature of container image tags to serve different content at different times. Unlike content-addressable digests, tags (e.g., 'latest', 'v1.0', 'stable') can be reassigned to point to different image layers. An attacker who gains access to a container registry account can replace the image behind a tag with a malicious version. Users pulling by tag receive the malicious image while believing they have the legitimate version.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: Multiple container supply chain attacks have exploited tag mutability. The Codecov compromise could serve modified containers by re-tagging images. Docker Hub has experienced unauthorized access incidents where image tags were potentially modified. Alpine Linux Docker images were briefly compromised in 2019.
supply_chain_attacks.affected_ecosystem: Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR, ACR, GCR, quay.io
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Deployment of malicious container images that appear legitimate. All systems pulling the affected tag receive the compromised image. Particularly dangerous for base images used across many applications.
detection_methods: Use image digests (@sha256:...) instead of tags
Implement container image scanning before deployment
Monitor for tag reassignment events in registry audit logs
Use Sigstore cosign to verify image signatures
mitigations: Always reference container images by digest, not tag
Sign container images using cosign or Notary v2
Implement admission controllers that verify image signatures before deployment
Use image allow-listing in deployment policies
Mirror critical base images in organization-controlled registries

supply_chain_attacks.attack_name: Abandoned Package Takeover via Registry Transfer
supply_chain_attacks.description: Attackers acquire control of abandoned or deprecated packages through legitimate registry mechanisms such as package name transfer requests, organization ownership changes, or registering packages whose names have been released. Once control is established, the attacker publishes a new version containing malicious code, which is automatically adopted by systems configured to accept minor or patch version updates.
supply_chain_attacks.case_study: npm's package transfer policy has been exploited to acquire abandoned packages. In multiple cases, attackers have requested ownership transfer of popular but unmaintained packages and subsequently published malicious versions. The 'getcookies' and 'express-cookies' incidents involved attacker-controlled packages that piggybacked on popular package names.
supply_chain_attacks.impact: Widespread distribution of malicious code through a previously trusted package name. Systems using version ranges (^, ~) in their dependency specifications automatically receive the malicious version.
detection_methods: Monitor for ownership changes on critical dependencies
Alert on new versions of previously dormant packages
Track maintainer changes through registry APIs
Monitor for unexpected download count spikes on old packages
mitigations: Pin exact dependency versions in lock files
Subscribe to security advisories for all dependencies
Audit dependencies for maintenance status and bus factor
Implement automated monitoring for dependency ownership changes
Use SCA tools that flag abandoned or transferred packages
